column4: The section itself identifies the exact reversal: God could have raised the sign-bearer, but he أَخْلَدَ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ, clung to earth; bodily height and ground-contact expose the spiritual fall into denial.
The face-down walker مُكِبًّا عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ is set against one who walks سَوِيًّا on a straight path, turning the section's upright-versus-lowered body into a moral and eschatological contrast.

Solomon's dead body remains upright only through his staff; when the creature eats the staff he falls, a uniquely concrete Quranic scene of a body, its support, and the collapse that follows support's removal.

The hypocrites' impressive bodies are likened to خُشُبٌ مُّسَنَّدَةٌ, propped timbers; external uprightness depends on a support while inwardly they are lifeless, sharpening the section's distinction between form and final rank.

After creating people, God takes them in death, and some are يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ; the same return-root and a bodily descent into decrepitude closely enact being returned from fine formation to a low condition.

This ayah joins creation from dust, embryonic formation, being returned to the most abject age, death, and revived earth as proof of resurrection; it contains nearly the whole section's rise-decline-ground-rise circuit.
وَمَن نُّعَمِّرْهُ نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ pictures long life as being reversed in bodily creation, a direct parallel to the upright body being turned downward.
God makes weakness, then strength, then weakness and gray hair; this explicitly identifies the sustaining strength between two bodily low states and attributes every transition to the same Creator.
The section cites this complete earth-cycle: created from earth, returned into it, and brought out from it once more; the body that reaches the ground will be raised again.
ثُمَّ يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا states both return into earth and forceful emergence from it, matching descent to the ground and the second rising.
The heavens and earth تَقُومَانِ by God's command, then humans answer a call and emerge from earth; cosmic standing-by-support and bodily resurrection meet in one ayah.
The section cites يَوْمَ يَقُومُ ٱلنَّاسُ لِرَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ: the root of bodily setting-upright culminates in all people standing for their Lord.
After the second trumpet blast, the dead are قِيَامٌ يَنظُرُونَ, standing and looking; this is the section's second upright posture after bodily return.
Faces are humbled before ٱلْحَىِّ ٱلْقَيُّومِ; the One by whom creation subsists confronts lowered human faces, joining the support-sense of the root to the final standing.
The command وَلَا تَقُمْ عَلَىٰ قَبْرِهِ places standing and the grave in one scene, while the dead person's disbelief makes it a pointed boundary for the section's faith exception.
The section cites the hypocrites in ٱلدَّرْكِ ٱلْأَسْفَلِ of the Fire, giving esfel an eschatological depth below bodily and social lowness.
Abraham's opponents intend to dominate him, but God makes them ٱلْأَسْفَلِينَ; the low rank is a divinely effected reversal, not merely a spatial description.
God makes the disbelievers' word ٱلسُّفْلَىٰ while His word is ٱلْعُلْيَا, an explicit rank-pair that confirms the section's upper/lower moral register.
The punished town's upper part is made its lower part, عَٰلِيَهَا سَافِلَهَا; the built structure is literally overturned across the same high/low axis developed in the section.
This repeated account again makes the town's عَالِيَهَا سَافِلَهَا, supplying a second direct occurrence of top becoming bottom.
The condemned ask to put their human and jinn misleaders beneath their feet so they become مِنَ ٱلْأَسْفَلِينَ; physical underfoot position and degraded rank coincide.
A ruined town lies collapsed on its roofs, a man is made to die and restored, and his bones are raised and clothed with flesh; fallen structure and reconstructed body illuminate one another.
The section cites the Creator who خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ, directly restating creation as bodily proportioning and balancing.
فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ completes 82:7 by locating that proportion in the deliberately assembled human form.
The abrupt answer كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ makes denial of judgment the response to fine formation, exactly the sequence the section highlights.
The section cites the rebuke to the garden owner: God created him from dust and a drop, then سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلًا; the completed man's stance is invoked against his disbelief.
Once Adam is proportioned and given spirit, the angels must prostrate; bodily completion becomes the threshold of a deliberate descent before the formed human.
The parallel command repeats فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُ and the breathing of spirit before prostration, confirming the completed upright human scene beyond its first telling.
God formed people and made their forms good, وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ, then states that the destination is to Him; good form and final return are held together.
Earth is made a settlement, heaven a structure, and human forms are made good; the ayah joins the body's fine form to the ground and built support imagery surrounding it.
ٱلَّذِىٓ أَحْسَنَ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقَهُ introduces human creation from clay, placing the section's 'best formation' within God's making creation well.
God proportions the human, breathes spirit, and grants hearing, sight, and hearts, yet people give little thanks; formed capacity is followed by a moral falling-short.
The embryo becomes bones, the bones are clothed with flesh, and it is produced as another creation; this makes the hidden construction behind the finished human body visible.
From a clot God خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ, created and proportioned the human; the wording directly parallels the section's account of making the body fit.
ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ states in compact form that creation includes setting in due proportion, the closest non-root equivalent of takwīm's forming work.
God says He created and then fashioned humankind before commanding the angels to prostrate to Adam; the formed body opens the same Adamic posture-scene as 15:29.
Creation from dust passes through embryo, childhood, maturity, old age, and death; this full bodily arc supplies the temporal descent implicit between finest formation and return.
Zechariah describes bones weakened and a head blazing with gray, giving the section's loss of bodily support a vivid first-person old-age form.
Believers who do good receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, the same uncut-reward formula as the section's exception.
This ayah exactly repeats both the exception for those who believe and do good and the promise أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ.
God promises the Prophet أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ, preserving the same uncut reward while changing the immediate addressee.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient receive their reward; this states in other words what 'uncut' reward adds to the image.
The blessed remain in the Garden with عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, a gift not cut off, an especially close nonlexical counterpart to ghayr mamnūn.
The section cites deniers as شَرُّ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ, making moral response turn created beings toward the worst rank.
The section's faithful exception is mirrored by believers who do good becoming خَيْرُ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ, the opposite human rank to 98:6.
إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَفِى خُسْرٍ gives another universal low outcome for humanity, whose exception is supplied by the next ayah.
The exception for faith, good works, truth, and patience closely parallels the section's movement from humanity's descent to those exempted through faith and deeds.
Wealth is called what God made قِيَٰمًا for people, a direct Quranic use of the q-w-m family for the means by which human life is supported.
God makes the Kaaba قِيَٰمًا لِّلنَّاسِ, a sustaining order for people; it expands the section's 'that by which a thing stands' from body to community.
ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ neither slumbers nor sleeps and possesses all things, giving the q-w-m root its supreme sustaining referent behind every dependent upright creature.
God holds the heavens and earth أَن تَزُولَا, lest they slip or fall, and none can hold them after Him; this directly matches support that turns a thing back from collapse.
God يُمْسِكُ ٱلسَّمَآءَ أَن تَقَعَ عَلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ, holds the sky from falling to earth, staging the exact relation between support, fall, and the ground.
God attacks a building from its foundations so its roof falls upon its occupants from above; withdrawn support converts the upper structure into a downward blow.
God raises the heavens بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ تَرَوْنَهَا, without visible pillars; height immediately raises the question of the support by which something elevated remains standing.
The heavens are created without visible pillars and stabilizing mountains are cast into earth lest it shift with people; cosmic and earthly supports frame the human standing-place.
God places no عِوَجًا, crookedness, in the Book; this is the removal of crookedness half of the section's definition of setting something upright.
قَيِّمًا completes 18:1: the Book is upright, warns of severe punishment, and announces good reward to believers who do good.
The command to set one's face to the religion joins God's human fiṭrah, no alteration in creation, and ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ; created form and moral uprightness meet explicitly.
The Quran guides لِلَّتِى هِىَ أَقْوَمُ and promises believers who do good a great reward, moving the upright-root from bodily form to the way that sustains a life.
Those who say 'Our Lord is God' and then ٱسْتَقَٰمُوا۟ are promised freedom from fear and the Garden; steadfast uprightness realizes the faithful exception.
When called to rise and go forth, people ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ and prefer worldly life; this is the closest nonlexical repeat of choosing to cling heavily to earth.
This preceding ayah identifies the man in 7:176 as one given signs who stripped himself from them; it supplies the lost support that makes his earthward fall a denial-scene.
Adam and his spouse are made to descend, with earth assigned as settlement and temporary provision; human life begins on the very ground to which the body returns.
The command ٱهْبِطُوا۟ sends humans down, and earth becomes their settlement and provision for a term, explicitly binding descent to the human ground.
On earth people live, die, and from it are brought forth; the ayah completes the descent of 7:24 with the same grave-and-second-rise circle as the section.
Deniers ask whether, once ضَلَلْنَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ, lost into the earth, they can be newly created; bodily disappearance into ground is explicitly tied to denial of meeting the Lord.
The skeptics ask whether they will be لَمَرْدُودُونَ فِى ٱلْحَافِرَةِ, returned to the former state; r-d-d here names resurrection as restoration.
The objection 'when we are decayed bones?' supplies the bodily condition from which the return questioned in 79:10 must occur.
The disputant forgets his own creation and asks who will revive decayed bones, making denial arise from failure to read the formed body backward to its Maker.
The answer says the One who originated the bones the first time will revive them, linking first formation directly to second formation.
The deniers' astonished question asks whether after becoming dust they will enter a new creation; the ayah then names them deniers of their Lord.
The objection أَءِذَا مِتْنَا وَكُنَّا تُرَابًا rejects a bodily return from dust as remote, placing the section's earthward return at the center of resurrection denial.
Humanity asks whether God will gather its bones, a direct denial of the body's reassembly after its collapse.
God answers that He can proportion even the fingertips, carrying fine bodily formation through death into exact re-formation.
God will raise those in the graves, directly turning the section's dictionary sense of balad as grave-ground into the place of bodily emergence.
At the trumpet people rush from the graves to their Lord; emergence from ground terminates in the standing for God developed through q-w-m.
With humbled eyes, people emerge from graves like scattered locusts; lowered faces and upward emergence appear in the same resurrection body.
People emerge rapidly from graves as though racing toward a marker, giving the second rising a forceful bodily movement.
God causes the human to die and assigns him a grave, the precise bodily lodging suggested by the section's secondary sense of balad.
ثُمَّ إِذَا شَآءَ أَنشَرَهُ reverses 80:21's burial by raising the same human when God wills.
When the graves are overturned and their contents scattered, the ground no longer holds the lowered bodies placed within it.
The earth splits away from people as they hasten out, a direct picture of ground releasing the bodies returned to it.
The earth casts out what is inside it and empties, continuing the section's ground image into the resurrection release.
The earth brings out its burdens, a compact image of buried bodies no longer remaining below.
God asks whether He made earth كِفَاتًا, a containing receptacle, making the ground a support and enclosure.
أَحْيَآءً وَأَمْوَٰتًا specifies that the earth of 77:25 gathers both living and dead bodies.
Rain is driven to a dead بَلَد and revives it, and the ayah says 'thus We bring out the dead'; the land-word's ground sense becomes an explicit resurrection analogy.
God revives a dead بَلَد with rain and concludes كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ, making dead land a direct figure for bodily rising.
Measured water revives a dead بَلْدَة, followed by كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ; the same ground that receives becomes the image of being brought out.
A dead بَلْدَة is given life and the ayah concludes كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ, explicitly joining land and emergence.
Rain revives a dead بَلْدَة and waters animals and people, showing the land not only as the body's bottom surface but as the support that restores bodily life.

Abraham asks that this be a secure بَلَد and that believers receive provision; the reply grants a disbeliever brief enjoyment before driving him to Fire, joining safe ground, sustenance, and final descent.
Abraham's prayer رَبِّ ٱجْعَلْ هَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدَ ءَامِنًا is the closest repeated formulation of the section's 'this secure city.'
A city secure and tranquil with abundant provision becomes clothed in hunger and fear after ingratitude; the secure ground is reversed by moral failure.
لَآ أُقْسِمُ بِهَٰذَا ٱلْبَلَدِ repeats the oath by 'this city,' activating the same named place before the bodily meanings the section hears beneath balad.
God makes a sanctuary secure while people are snatched away around it, then asks whether they believe in falsehood; physical security is again placed beside denial.
The same divine hand gives and removes rule, honors and abases; this rank reversal closely matches the section's hand that supports and lowers.
A person's wealth will not avail إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ, when he falls; material support fails at the decisive downward movement.
One who associates partners is likened to a person falling from the sky and carried off by birds or wind, giving loss of faith the section's unsupported bodily fall.
True believers in the signs خَرُّوا۟ سُجَّدًا when reminded and are not arrogant; voluntary bodily lowering becomes the opposite of the denier's degrading fall.
The command وَٱسْجُدْ وَٱقْتَرِب makes going down to the ground the means of drawing near, reversing any simple equation of physical height with spiritual rank.
The coming event is خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ, lowering some and raising others; it states the final two-way rank reversal latent in the section's vertical axis.
God raises believers and people of knowledge by degrees; this is the faithful upward counter-movement to being placed among the low.
Whoever comes as a believer with righteous deeds receives ٱلدَّرَجَٰتُ ٱلْعُلَىٰ, the high degrees, an explicit upper-rank counterpart to the section's low destination and faithful exception.
The final abode is for those who do not desire عُلُوًّا in the earth; it marks a boundary between gifted uprightness and self-exalting rank.
People who refuse to use their created faculties become like cattle, indeed further astray; fine human equipment can terminate in a rank below the creaturely comparison.
The question أَلَا يَظُنُّ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ أَنَّهُم مَّبْعُوثُونَ introduces the resurrection whose bodily standing is shown in 83:6.
This ayah names the setting as a tremendous day, giving the standing in 83:6 its judicial scale even though it does not itself picture the posture.
God caused humankind to grow from earth like a growth; read with 71:18, origin in the ground precedes return into and emergence from it.
Adam's likeness begins from dust before God's creative command, a concise origin-from-ground counterpart to the body's eventual return.
Creation from dust is followed by humans spreading across the earth, moving from low material origin to active embodied life.
Creation from dust and then a drop is followed by the measured span of every life, placing formed embodiment under the same power that limits its duration.
God creates the human from a mixed drop in order to test him and equips him with hearing and sight; fine formation is explicitly ordered toward moral trial.
Guidance leaves the formed human either grateful or ungrateful, clarifying how one created form can lead to the section's opposed final ranks.
God creates death and life to test who is best in deeds; 'best' shifts from received bodily form to the action by which that form is answered.
Creation of the human from a clinging clot begins a short passage that soon shows the created person imagining himself independent.
كَلَّآ إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ لَيَطْغَىٰ marks the formed human's moral overreach, the start of the downward turn completed by the next ayat.
The human transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient, a direct spiritual denial of the section's claim that standing always depends on a sustaining power.
إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ٱلرُّجْعَىٰ restores the dependence denied in 96:7 by naming the unavoidable return to the Lord.
Humans are the needy before God while God is self-sufficient and praiseworthy; this supplies the theological relation behind a body that cannot uphold itself.
قَوَّٰمُونَ names an ongoing human maintenance responsibility and grounds it partly in spending, another concrete social use of the root for sustaining others.
Balanced spending is قَوَامًا between extravagance and stinginess, extending the root from bodily poise to a measure that keeps conduct from leaning to either extreme.
Revelation and the balance are sent so that people لِيَقُومَ ٱلنَّاسُ بِٱلْقِسْطِ, making 'standing' the establishment of a just human order.
The command كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ turns sustained uprightness into a stance for justice even against oneself and kin.
Believers are commanded to be قَوَّٰمِينَ لِلَّهِ as witnesses in justice, another moral stance held upright despite hostility.
Those who say God is their Lord and then ٱسْتَقَٰمُوا۟ have no fear or grief; it repeats the faithful consequence of remaining upright.
The message is for whoever wills أَن يَسْتَقِيمَ, carrying the bodily root into the human choice to take a straight course.
Remembering God while standing, sitting, and lying on one's side distinguishes qiyām as a concrete bodily posture among the alternatives implied by the section.
After prayer, believers remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides; the repeated posture triad confirms the root's simplest physical sense.
When hardship touches a person he calls on God lying, sitting, or standing, then passes on after relief; shifting bodily states accompany forgetfulness of the sustaining hand.
The devout person spends the night prostrating and standing while fearing the Hereafter, a faithful alternation of lowered and upright postures rather than a degrading fall.
God raises the heaven and sets the balance, joining height to the measured order that keeps it from becoming distortion.
The command وَأَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلْوَزْنَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ uses the standing-root for maintaining just measure, a nonbodily analogue to corrected, balanced form.
God raises the heaven's canopy and proportions it, transferring the section's two linked acts—elevation and setting right—from the body to a structure.
The disbelieving garden owner's crop is destroyed and its trellised growth lies collapsed, so the rebuke about the One who formed him in 18:37 ends in a visible loss of support.
Destroyed towns lie collapsed upon their roofs, repeating at civic scale the downward result of a structure losing what holds it up.
مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ pictures a destitute person pressed into dust, a concrete meeting of low social rank and bodily nearness to earth.
Paradise fruit is لَا مَقْطُوعَةٍ وَلَا مَمْنُوعَةٍ, neither cut off nor withheld, making the section's 'uncut' reward sensuous without sharing the m-n-n form.
The Garden's food and shade are lasting, a concrete statement of the continuance conveyed by ghayr mamnūn.
God's provision in the Hereafter has no exhaustion, مَا لَهُۥ مِن نَّفَادٍ, another explicit boundary against a reward that ends.
The patient are paid their reward without reckoning, extending the faithful exception toward a gift unbounded by ordinary measure.
God honors Adam's children, carries and provides for them, and favors them over much creation; this states the bestowed human rank surrounding 'best formation.'
Punishment can come from above or from beneath people's feet, marking both sides of the vertical boundary on which the section's bodily image rests.
Punishment covers deniers from above and from beneath their feet, enclosing the body between upper and lower rather than leaving its height secure.
Criminals stand with heads bowed before their Lord and ask to be sent back; forced lowering at judgment contrasts with the confident upright form they once misused.
On the day of warning people rush with heads raised while their gaze لَا يَرْتَدُّ إِلَيْهِمْ; the return-root now describes an eye unable to come back under terror.
Those given knowledge fall on their faces in prostration when revelation is recited, making bodily descent the truthful answer to God's signs.
Prophets and the guided خَرُّوا۟ سُجَّدًا وَبُكِيًّا when God's signs are recited; falling to earth here manifests elevated faith rather than degradation.
The contents of the graves are scattered out, directly continuing the section's grave-ground image into bodily exposure at judgment.
The crow scratches the earth to show Cain how to cover his brother's corpse, supplying the Quran's first concrete scene of a human body being put into the ground.
Worldly rivalry continues until people visit the graves; bodily arrival in cemetery-ground terminates the self-exalting contest.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him, compressing first formation, re-formation, and final return into one ayah.
The return of all to God is guaranteed because He begins and repeats creation; the repeated creation then separates righteous believers' reward from deniers' punishment.
God gives life to the dead, causes death, gives life again, and to Him people are returned; the whole bodily circuit belongs to one sustaining hand.
God promises to repeat creation just as He began the first creation, making the second formation answer directly to the first well-formed body.
إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ attributes both origination and repetition to the same agent, a compact statement of the section's creation-return relation.
When skeptics ask who will restore them, the answer is the One who formed them the first time; first bodily formation is the warrant for return.
At death the human asks, 'My Lord, return me,' making r-d-d's restoration sense a desperate bodily request at the point of collapse.
The requested return is refused, a barrier remains until resurrection, and the speaker's wish to do righteousness connects bodily return with the faithful exception.
God takes souls at death and sleep, retains those decreed to die, and sends the others back for a term; the same hand withholds and restores bodily life.
The human was first a discharged drop, supplying the low material beginning for the created and proportioned body in 75:38.
After recalling first formation, the passage asks whether its Maker can revive the dead; fine form becomes the direct proof of re-formation.
The question asks the human what deceived him concerning his generous Lord, framing the bodily forming in 82:7-8 and denial in 82:9 as one rebuke.
After creating and proportioning in 87:2, God measures and guides; fitting form is joined to an assigned measure and course.
God has created people in successive stages, supplying the developmental movement between earthly origin and the return-and-emergence of 71:17-18.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, giving the formed body in 23:14 its material origin in earth.
The drop is placed in a firm lodging, a concrete support and enclosure within the process that produces the completed body in 23:14.
The oath by the soul and the One who proportioned it moves the section's fitted form inward, from bodily balance to the human self.
The proportioned self is shown both its wickedness and its piety, explaining how one created form opens toward opposed moral ranks.
Success belongs to the one who purifies the proportioned self, a close ethical counterpart to the section's faithful exception.
Failure belongs to the one who corrupts or buries the self, giving the moral fall an earthward verb after the self's proportioning.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and grants hearing, sight, and hearts, yet little gratitude follows; bestowed equipment can end in moral failure.
God produces human hearing, sight, and hearts, followed by 'little are you grateful'; completed capacities do not guarantee an upright response.
The Creator produces people and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, but they give little thanks; human formation and human failure stand side by side.
God creates people from clay and fixes both a life-term and an appointed term with Him, yet the addressees still doubt; earth-origin leads directly to judgment-denial.
God produced humans from earth and settled them in it, then calls them to seek forgiveness and return; earth is both origin, habitation, and setting for moral response.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are called worst in place and most astray in path, merging bodily inversion with degraded final rank.
The criminals are dragged on their faces into the Fire, a literal final lowering of bodies that rejected resurrection.
Those who bring evil are thrown face-first into the Fire; the downward bodily orientation realizes their low moral outcome.
The condemned are gathered on their faces, blind, mute, and deaf, with Hell as refuge; honored human faculties and upright carriage are comprehensively reversed.
On the day people are summoned to prostrate, they cannot do so; the once-sound upright body has lost the capacity for faithful voluntary lowering.
Eyes are humbled and humiliation covers those who were called to prostrate while sound, distinguishing chosen prostration in life from forced abasement at judgment.
When the Quran is recited, the addressees do not prostrate; refusal to lower the body before revelation becomes a sign of the deeper fall.
The next ayah identifies the refusal as denial, explicitly tying bodily non-prostration to the same تكذيب challenged in surah 95.
Those who recognize revelation fall on their faces weeping and increase in humility, completing the truthful bodily response begun in 17:107.
The command to descend to earth is followed by promised guidance and freedom from fear for those who follow it, giving the earthly descent its faithful boundary.
Those who disbelieve and deny the signs become companions of the Fire, completing the same descent passage with the opposite outcome.
Humans are sent down together, but whoever follows divine guidance will neither stray nor suffer; descent to earth does not itself determine low moral rank.
Satan is ordered to descend because proud self-exaltation has no place there and is told to leave among the abased, joining direction, arrogance, and low rank.
Good speech ascends to God and righteous action raises it, giving good deeds an upward movement opposite the denier's attachment to earth.
A building founded on reverence is opposed to one on a collapsing brink that falls with its builder into Hell; sound support and final downward collapse form the whole comparison.
A good word is a good tree whose root is firm and branch reaches heaven, a living image of upright height sustained from below and bearing continuing fruit.
An evil word is an uprooted tree with no stability in the earth, showing how loss of grounding turns apparent height into collapse.
The believers are likened to a crop that strengthens its shoots, thickens, and stands upright on its stems; mutual support produces a mature upright form.
People once stood on the brink of a pit of Fire, but God saved them as they held His rope together; divine and communal support prevent the terminal fall.
Iram is identified with lofty pillars, the very structural object named in the section as the support that holds something upright.
God wills to confer favor on those weakened in the earth and make them leaders and inheritors; the m-n-n family accompanies a divinely effected rise of the lowly into strength.
Good land brings forth vegetation by its Lord's leave while bad land yields only scant growth; the same ground bears opposed outcomes according to its condition.
A good land and forgiving Lord accompany two productive gardens and provision, showing balad as sustaining ground rather than merely a named city.
When the people turn away, their fertile gardens are replaced after the flood by bitter, sparse growth; sustaining land visibly falls from good condition.
Abraham's standing-place and the safety of whoever enters the sanctuary meet in one ayah, linking q-w-m's place-form to the secure city.
The House is made a place of return and security, and Abraham's standing-place a place of prayer; return, safety, and q-w-m converge at the sanctuary.
The Lord of the House feeds people against hunger and secures them against fear, specifying the bodily sustenance contained in the image of a secure city.
At resurrection the mountains are removed and the ground is left a level plain, stripping the standing-place of its former elevations and supports.
No crookedness or uneven rise can be seen in the leveled ground, a cosmic counterpart to removing crookedness and the final erasure of high/low terrain.
People are presented before God in rows and told they have come as first created, making first formation and final standing one explicit judicial scene.
When earth and heavens are exchanged, everyone appears before the One God; even the body's ground is remade for the final presentation.
A single blast is sufficient for resurrection, the initiating act whose bodily result appears in the next ayah.
After the blast, people are suddenly upon the earth's surface, an especially concise emergence from below to above.
The earth is stretched out before casting out what lies within it, preparing a level ground for the release described in 84:4.
The earth is shaken with its final convulsion before bringing out its burdens, so the supporting ground itself moves at bodily emergence.
The passage first identifies the one who transgressed, beginning the downward moral sequence that culminates in Fire.
Preferring the nearer life supplies the concrete choice behind the transgressor's low outcome.
Hell becomes the transgressor's refuge, the lower eschatological terminus of preferring worldly life.
The opposite person fears the standing before his Lord and restrains the self from desire; q-w-m's judicial sense produces an upright moral response.
The Garden becomes that person's refuge, completing the faithful upward alternative to 79:39.
People prefer the worldly life, a specific choice of the nearer and passing condition that parallels clinging to earth.
The Hereafter is better and more enduring, stating the lasting counterpart to the section's uncut reward.
Those content with worldly life, at rest in it, and heedless of the signs enact the earth-bound satisfaction that precedes denial's low end.
Fire is their refuge because of what they earned, completing the passage's movement from worldly contentment to final abasement.
At death the life reaches the collarbones, locating the body's loss of strength within the body itself.
One leg is entwined with the other, a vivid image of the formerly upright body's support failing at death.
On that day the drive is toward the Lord, turning bodily collapse into the unavoidable final return.
Earth is made a resting spread and sky a canopy, followed by provision; the human body's standing-place and covering are explicitly supplied by God.
Earth is made a resting-place, the broad support beneath the upright human body.
Mountains are made pegs, completing 78:6's ground with the image of what fixes and stabilizes it.
Firm mountains are cast into earth lest it shift with people, directly showing the standing-ground secured against collapse.
Firm mountains keep earth from shifting with its inhabitants, a repeated formulation of the support beneath embodied human movement.
Deniers are made to stand before their Lord, acknowledge the truth, and face punishment; rejected judgment becomes an actual presentation.
The human labors toward the Lord and will meet Him, making the body's whole exertion terminate in return and encounter.
God makes earth tractable for walking and provision, then says resurrection is to Him; the supporting ground of life leads directly to emergence.
God makes humans successors in earth and raises some over others in degrees to test them, distinguishing divinely assigned rank from moral worth.
Worldly preference already creates ranks, but the Hereafter has greater degrees and preference; final rank exceeds visible bodily and social height.
God raises Jesus and places his followers above disbelievers until resurrection, then all return for judgment; raising, rank, return, and verdict form one promise.
The deaf and speechless who do not reason are called the worst creatures before God, a moral low rank reached despite human form.
Those who refuse to hear or reason become like cattle, indeed further astray, repeating the fall beneath the rank implied by human formation.
The living and dead are not equal, and the Prophet cannot make those in graves hear; grave-ground marks a present boundary that resurrection alone will reverse.
Moses says he leans upon his staff, giving the support-object from Solomon's fall scene its ordinary bodily function.
The Fire closes upon its inmates in extended columns; a pillar that ordinarily supports becomes part of the enclosure of the fallen.
The Prophet is told not to give or remind of a favor seeking increase; this distinct m-n-n sense sets human calculated giving against God's uncut reward.
A secure sanctuary receives provision from God, repeating the safe-ground and sustenance pairing without the word balad.
The Prophet is described in relation to 'this city,' continuing 90:1's oath and locating the addressee within the same named ground; the precise nuance of حِلٌّ is not relied upon here.
People love the immediate life, naming the temporal preference behind the earthward attachment.
They leave the Hereafter, completing the boundary between passing nearness and enduring reward.
God raises some people above others in degrees so that they may take one another in service, showing social height as an interdependent support-order rather than self-sufficiency.
When Joseph's shirt reaches Jacob's face, he returns to seeing; فَٱرْتَدَّ بَصِيرًا is an exact bodily example of r-d-d restoring a prior condition.
Wealth and children are passing adornment, while enduring righteous deeds are better in reward and hope; what passes is measured against what remains.
Enduring righteous deeds are better with God in reward and return, repeating the lasting consequence of the faithful exception.
Believers are commanded to stand before God devoutly, making created upright posture an act of worship before its final judicial form.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord, using both lowered and upright postures in faithful devotion.
